newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: LABOR'S PURSUIT OF PROSSER TO CONTINUE
Federal Small Business Minister, Geoff Prosser, is likely to be questioned in parliament today about his investments in West Australian shopping centres.
The Opposition claims these investments create a conflict of interest, because Mr Prosser's portfolio includes responsibilities relating to policy on franchisees.
Labor says this means Mr Prosser has breached the Ministerial Code of Conduct.
Mr Prosser says if a conflict did arise, the relevant issue would pass to his senior Ministerial colleague, John Moore.
Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, has dismissed this defence, and he says the Ministerial Code of Conduct is a vague veil.
Mr Beazley says the current government has the lowest standards of any in the past two decades, and is likely to use question time today to demand Mr Prosser either stands down or be sacked.
LABOR HAPPY TO TAKE PART IN TAX REFORM DEBATE
Federal Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says Labor is opposed to a goods and services tax, which he says would be a job destroyer that damages families.
But Mr Beazley says the Opposition has not ruled out consideration of any other tax reform measures the Government may come up with.
He says a GST would attack small businesses and families, two constituencies claimed by the Prime Minister.
His comments follow a meeting of Coalition M-Ps last night to discuss tax reform.
This morning, Treasurer Peter Costello, said debate about the need for tax reform, and the possible introduction of a goods and services tax, should not be delayed any longer.
It is a challenge Mr Beazley says he is happy to accept.
FEARS THAT BOATPEOPLE WILL NOT GET A FAIR HEARING
A refugee advocacy group fears the latest group of people to enter the Port Hedland Detention Centre will be sent home without being given a proper hearing.
A total of 136 boatpeople who arrived on Thursday Island off the Queensland coast last week have been transported to Port Hedland.
Another three are due to arrive today.
The Immigration Department has sent 16 staff to interview them.

The West Australian representative on the Independent Council for Refugee Advocacy, Richard Egan, says each person will only be asked two questions and will not have the chance to put their case for refugee status.
He says they will just be asked why they left their country and why they came to Australia.
CALL FOR RADAR SYSTEM TO MONITOR IMMIGRATION WATERS
The Federal Opposition says the Jindalee over-the-horizon radar system should be an integral part of Australia's guard against illegal immigrants.
Labor's Defence Spokesman, Arch Bevis, says the multi-million dollar system, with bases at Longreach in Queensland, and Laverton in Western Australia, still is not operational.
Mr Bevis says the government should be throwing its support behind the project, and make it part of Australia's co-ordinated effort to stop illegal immigration.
He says it is a very large coastline to monitor, which is one thing the Jindalee system will be very good at doing.
He says Jindalee could give immigration authorities a pretty good picture of what is moving in waters to Australia's north.
WHALE WATCHING DISTANCE LIMIT "TOO LOW"
There is criticism of Environment Ministers from around Australia over their decision to set a 50 metre limit for whale watching.
The Ministers met in Cairns to set the limit for observation boats.
South Australia's Whale Centre says more distance is needed. Steve Vines, a member of the Australian Dolphin Research Foundation, who operates a dolphin-watching business on the Port River, agrees.
Mr Vines says the new limit fails to understand that while creatures, such as dolphins, are happy to get very close to boats, many whales would feel harassed.
He says the decision may please some eco-tourism opertors, but, for others, it is not appropriate.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
